analysis.one_liner: Raises civil penalties for securities fraud and adds tougher penalties for repeat offenders.
analysis.headline: Four senators from both parties sponsored a bill to raise securities fraud penalties, but it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in March 2017 and never received another action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have sharply increased the civil fines the SEC and federal courts can impose on people and companies that violate securities laws. It raised the dollar caps across four major securities statutes, added a new top tier of penalties for fraud that causes large investor losses, tripled penalties for repeat offenders, and made each day of ignoring an SEC order a separate violation. It died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors and retirement savers who lose money to securities fraud would benefit from stronger deterrence: the bill made fraud that causes substantial investor losses punishable by up to $10 million per violation or triple the wrongdoer's gain or the victims' losses, whichever is greater. It also gave the SEC more leverage by tripling penalties for repeat offenders and by treating each day of violating an SEC bar or court injunction as a separate offense. Honest financial firms would also gain from competing in a market where cheating is costlier.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the civil penalty caps for securities violations across four statutes — the Securities Act of 1933, the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, the Investment Company Act of 1940, and the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 — so top-tier penalties for companies rise from $500,000 to $10 million per violation, or triple the wrongdoer's gain or the victims' losses when fraud causes substantial harm.

Adds a fourth penalty tier that triples the maximum fine for any person who, within the previous five years, was criminally convicted of securities fraud or was already subject to an SEC fraud order — targeting repeat offenders specifically.

Makes each separate violation of a federal court injunction, SEC bar, or cease-and-desist order a separate offense, with each day of continued noncompliance counted separately, so firms cannot simply absorb a one-time fine and keep violating.

analysis.who_pays: Financial firms, brokerages, investment advisers, and executives that commit securities fraud would bear higher fines. Compliance and settlement costs would partly spread to firms' shareholders and customers, as is the case with any penalty regime, but the bill's tiers are aimed at fraud, manipulation, and deliberate or reckless rule-breaking rather than routine business activity.
analysis.who_pays_short: Securities fraud offenders and financial firms

drawbacks.text: The third-tier penalty can reach the full amount of victims' losses or triple the wrongdoer's gain, whichever is greater, and violations of SEC orders are counted per day — so penalties can accumulate to amounts far beyond any fixed cap, which critics argue pushes firms to settle cases regardless of merit rather than contest them.

Penalties imposed on a public company are ultimately paid from the company itself, meaning diversified shareholders — including ordinary investors with index funds — can end up bearing part of the cost of penalties aimed at the firm's wrongdoing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are well targeted: higher, escalating penalties for fraud, repeat offenders, and firms that ignore SEC orders fall mainly on wrongdoers and strengthen the SEC's ability to settle cases on terms that deter the next violation. The main honest concern is that loss-based and per-day penalties can grow very large and that public shareholders share in penalties paid by their companies. On balance the design is a moderate, conventional strengthening of enforcement rather than an extreme measure, which makes its quiet death in committee harder to justify.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed introduced the bill on March 30, 2017 with three cosponsors from both parties — Republican Chuck Grassley and Democrats Heidi Heitkamp and Patrick Leahy.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, the committee that handles securities law.
The bill received no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — for the rest of the 115th Congress.
When the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, the bill expired with it, as any bill not passed by both chambers does.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial firms and executives exposed to securities fraud claims are better off, because the higher penalty regime never took effect. The Banking Committee leadership is also better off, having avoided a recorded vote on a bill with bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.role: Chairman, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the bill shows no committee action after its referral.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — three Democrats and one Republican sponsored the bill — but because the Banking Committee never acted, there was never a vote that would show how the parties lined up in opposition.

industries.industry: Wall Street banks, brokerages, and securities firms
industries.note: The bill would have raised the maximum civil penalty for fraud to $10 million per violation or triple the firm's gain or victims' losses, making securities fraud substantially more expensive. Because the bill died, the existing lower penalty structure stayed in place.

industries.industry: Investment advisers and mutual fund managers
industries.note: The bill raised penalty caps under both the Investment Advisers Act and the Investment Company Act and tripled penalties for advisers with recent fraud records. Advisers who commit fraud benefit from the bill's failure; honest advisers would have gained a cleaner competitive field.

industries.industry: Corporate executives subject to SEC orders
industries.note: Executives already barred or ordered by the SEC would have faced tripled penalties for new violations and per-day penalties for ignoring orders. Only individuals and firms with prior fraud records or existing orders are affected, so compliant executives lose nothing.
